title: It’s Contract Renewal Season, But Some Customers Aren’t Biting
summary: My colleagues and I have been hearing a lot of stories about big enterprise customers renegotiating their annual contracts with model developers. Traditionally, software sellers use this time as an opportunity to convince customers to increase their annual commit by, for instance, reminding them how they exceeded their usage limits this year or highlighting new features they’ve released. In the past, model developers have had success using that playbook. This year has been a different story, though, some customers tell me. For instance, one executive at a major financial services firm said their company was hesitant to increase their spending commitment with Anthropic , OpenAI or any other model provider for a couple reasons. First, this executive said, the rapid pace of model releases means enterprises want flexibility to quickly switch to whatever the best new model is, something that can change week to week.

title: How Smugglers Get Expensive Memory Chips to China from South Korea
summary: For an illustration of how porous U.S. restrictions on the shipment of AI chips to China can be, consider a technique that has begun to catch on among smugglers involving a key type of memory chip. While U.S. export regulations ban the shipment of high-bandwidth memory chips on their own to China, including from countries like South Korea, those rules have a loophole that allows the sales of those memory chips if they’re packaged together on plates with cheap server processors whose performance falls below the export restriction threshold. That’s because the computing power of the package gets determined by the server processor, not the memory chips, according to the rules.

title: Apple’s Slowdown

The script for his first earnings call on Monday was so full of marketing palaver about Apple products, and so lacking in information, that Ternus’ predecessor, Tim Cook, must have been glowing with pride. Perhaps after seeing investors freak out last week when other big tech firms reported earnings squeezed by AI investments, Ternus was determined to bore Wall Street into submission. Alas! Finance chief Kevan Parekh woke listeners from their Ternus-induced slumber by projecting 7% to 10% growth in revenue for the December quarter, a marked slowdown from the 12% growth in the September period. Meanwhile, he projected a drop in Apple’s gross margin, thanks to rising costs of memory. Apple shares promptly traded down, falling as much as 4% in after-hours trading. Parekh blamed limited component supplies for the expected revenue slowdown: Apple can’t make as many of its devices as it could sell. But that may not be the only explanation.

( The full episode is available here .) The institute is one of the world’s largest government bodies focused on AI, and its work includes evaluating models from leading AI companies.

title: Inside Apple’s Slog to Create Its First Robot
summary: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots, but judging by Apple’s plodding progress on the first one it hopes to sell—a device with a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp—he could face an uphill battle. Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it. The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get off a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it. Much of the hardware needed for the robot has been finished for around two years, but the software team has found it difficult to keep pace, people who have worked on the project said. The hardware team responsible for J595 has pushed to hurry up and release the product. Meanwhile, the software team has advocated for delaying its release, and for the past year, it has attempted to strip back some proposed features and focus the product on a few capabilities related to FaceTime and automating home tasks, like switching on a light.
